lessons.title: Reading and responding to workplace documents
lessons.html:
Interpreting written communication

Every farm and extension office runs on written communication: work instructions, spray programmes, memos, circulars from the provincial department, SMS and WhatsApp messages, safety notices, product labels, letters from farmers and emails from suppliers. Misreading one of them can cost money or cause harm, for example spraying the wrong block or missing a deadline for a drought-relief application.

A method for reading workplace documents

  1. Purpose: Why was this written? To inform, instruct, request or persuade?
  2. Audience: Is it meant for you, your team or the whole organisation?
  3. Main message: Summarise it in one sentence in your own words.
  4. Action: What must be done, by whom and by when?
  5. Details: Check names, dates, quantities, block numbers and amounts in ZAR.
  6. Unclear points: Note questions and ask the sender rather than guessing.

Fact and opinion

Separate facts that can be checked (the borehole delivered 2 000 litres per hour on test) from opinions (the borehole is good enough). Notice tone too: a complaint letter from a farmer may be angry, but the facts in it still need to be checked and answered.

Responding

  • Respond within the time expected, even if only to say you received the message and when you will reply fully.
  • Answer every question asked, in the same order.
  • Use the channel that suits the matter: a quick WhatsApp to confirm a meeting time, a formal letter or email for a decision or a complaint.
  • Keep copies of important messages and replies on file.

Accessible communication means the reader can understand it easily. When you pass a message on to workers, translate it into plain language or their home language and check that they understood by asking them to explain it back.

lessons.title: Writing simple, clear workplace documents
lessons.html:
Producing written communication

Typical documents you will write include short reports on farm visits, memos to staff, notices for farmer days, minutes of meetings, emails to suppliers and incident reports.

Plan before you write

  • Who will read it, and what do they already know?
  • What do you want them to know or do after reading?
  • What format is expected: memo, letter, email, report or form?

Rules for clear writing

  1. Put the main point first.
  2. Use short sentences and everyday words: use instead of utilise, start instead of commence.
  3. One idea per paragraph; use numbered steps for instructions and bullet points for lists.
  4. Be specific: Meet at the dip tank on Tuesday 14 March at 08:00, not Meet next week in the morning.
  5. Avoid jargon and abbreviations unless the reader knows them.
  6. Be polite and neutral, even when the topic is a complaint.
  7. Check spelling, names, numbers and dates before sending.

Example: a short notice

Farmer day: managing ticks in winter

  • Date: Thursday 6 June, 09:00 to 12:00
  • Place: Community hall, next to the clinic
  • Bring: your livestock record book
  • Contact: the extension officer on the number on the office board

Example: a visit report outline

SectionContent
HeadingFarmer, place, date, enterprise
PurposeWhy the visit took place
FindingsWhat you observed and measured
Advice givenWhat was recommended
Follow-upActions, responsible person, date

Keep a professional standard on social media and messaging groups too. A message in a farmer WhatsApp group is a workplace document; it can be forwarded and kept.

lessons.title: Oral communication: speaking and listening at work
lessons.html:
Producing and responding to oral communication

Much of extension and farm work happens by word of mouth: briefing a team at the start of the day, phoning a supplier, speaking at a farmer day, taking part in a meeting with the traditional council, or calming an upset client.

Speaking clearly

  • Know your purpose and your main points before you start.
  • Use the language your audience understands best; use an interpreter if needed and allow time for translation.
  • Speak slowly and clearly, and use examples from the audience's own farms.
  • Use visual aids: a soil sample, a tick, a sample feed bag, a simple chart.
  • Check understanding by asking questions, not by asking Do you understand?
  • Show respect for cultural customs, such as greeting elders first and following meeting protocol.

Active listening

  1. Give your full attention; put the phone away.
  2. Let the speaker finish without interrupting.
  3. Show you are listening with eye contact (where culturally appropriate) and short responses.
  4. Ask open questions to get more information.
  5. Summarise what you heard: So the problem is that the calves are dying in the first week?
  6. Respond to feelings as well as facts.

Telephone and meetings

On the phone, greet, give your name and organisation, state the reason for the call, write down key details and confirm actions before ending. In meetings, prepare by reading the agenda, keep contributions short and on the topic, and note the decisions and who is responsible.

Handling difficult conversations

Stay calm, listen fully, acknowledge the person's concern, keep to the facts, explain what you can and cannot do, agree a next step, and follow up. If you cannot solve the matter, refer it to the right person and tell the client who that is.

Key points

  • Read workplace documents for purpose, main message, action and deadline, and ask when unclear.
  • Write with the main point first, short sentences and specific details.
  • Choose a channel and format that fit the message and the reader.
  • Speak in the audience's language and check understanding with questions.
  • Listen actively, summarise, and confirm agreed actions.

quiz.question: When reading a workplace instruction, what should you do if a point is unclear?
Which statement is a fact rather than an opinion?

options.text: The borehole delivered 2 000 litres per hour on test
The borehole is probably the best in the area
Meet next week in the morning
Meet soon at the usual place
We will commence the gathering at a time to be utilised
Meet at the dip tank on Tuesday 14 March at 08:00
